content: Active management of the third stage of labor (AMTSL) involves a series of interventions, including the administration of a prophylactic uterotonic (given at or after the delivery of the baby), clamping and cutting of the umbilical cord, controlled cord traction (CCT) to assist in delivering the placenta, and uterine massage. Recent guidelines recommend delaying cord clamping until the healthcare provider is ready to initiate CCT. The AMTSL approach has been shown to reduce the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), with the routine use of uterotonics being a key contributor to this reduction. However, the specific role of CCT in this process remains unclear. CCT can be uncomfortable for the patient, and some women may prefer a less interventional, hands-off approach. Additionally, implementing CCT requires training for healthcare providers, which has resource implications. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of controlled cord traction during the third stage of labor, either as part of conventional active management or as a standalone intervention. The researchers conducted a systematic search of relevant databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and PubMed, up to January 29, 2014. They included randomized controlled trials that compared planned CCT with no planned CCT in women undergoing vaginal delivery. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data using a standardized form. Three high-quality trials were included in the analysis, involving data from 199, 4,058, and 23,616 women, respectively. Blinding was not feasible in these studies, but the risk of bias was minimized by the objective measurement of blood loss. The results showed no significant difference in the risk of blood loss ≥ 1000 mL between the CCT and no-CCT groups (three trials, 27,454 women; risk ratio [RR] 0.91, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77 to 1.08). However, the use of CCT was associated with a reduction in the need for manual removal of the placenta (two trials, 27,665 women; RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.83). In the World Health Organization (WHO) trial, this reduction was primarily observed in settings where ergometrine was routinely used during the third stage of labor. A non-prespecified analysis excluding sites that routinely used ergometrine found no significant difference in the risk of manual placenta removal (one trial, 23,010 women; RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.46). In a French study, a policy limiting the third stage of labor to 30 minutes may have influenced the results (4,057 women; RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.90). Among secondary outcomes, CCT was associated with reductions in blood loss ≥ 500 mL (three trials, 27,454 women; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.88 to 0.99), mean blood loss (two trials, 27,255 women; mean difference [MD] -10.85 mL, 95% CI -16.73 to -4.98), and the duration of the third stage of labor (two trials, 27,360 women; standardized MD -0.57, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.54). There were no significant differences in the use of additional uterotonics (three trials, 27,829 women; average RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.02), blood transfusion, maternal death or severe morbidity, operative procedures, or maternal satisfaction. Maternal pain, a non-prespecified outcome, was reduced in one trial (3,760 women; RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.99). Several secondary outcomes were not reported in any of the trials, including retained placenta for more than 60 minutes, maternal hemoglobin levels below 9 g/dL at 24 to 48 hours post-delivery, organ failure, intensive care unit admission, caregiver satisfaction, cost-effectiveness, evacuation of retained products, or infection. The authors concluded that CCT has the benefit of reducing the risk of manual removal of the placenta in certain circumstances. Evidence supports the routine use of CCT during the third stage of labor, provided the birth attendant is adequately trained in the technique. CCT should remain a core competency for skilled birth attendants. However, the limited benefits of CCT in preventing severe PPH do not justify significant investments in training for healthcare providers who lack formal training in this skill. Women who prefer a less interventional approach can be reassured that when a uterotonic agent is used, omitting routine CCT from the active management package does not increase the risk of severe PPH, although it may increase the likelihood of manual placenta removal. Future research should explore the role of CCT in the absence of uterotonics and the potential contribution of uterine massage in managing the third stage of labor.
